The industrialization of AI: 8 critical considerations for building an AI gigafactory

The rapid rise of artificial intelligence has transcended the boundaries of corporate software innovation, sparking a foundational transformation in global infrastructure. Across the globe, nations, research institutions, and large enterprises are shifting away from traditional data center models toward massive, centralized hubs designed explicitly to industrialize AI workloads at an unprecedented scale.

As the European Commission works to establish multiple facilities dedicated to training next-generation AI models with trillions of parameters, a new term has emerged to describe these monumental engineering feats: the AI gigafactory.

While a standard corporate AI setup might utilize a few hundred or thousand GPUs, an AI gigafactory scales up to tens or hundreds of thousands of nodes. Power requirements shift dramatically from standard line-item budgeting to a fundamental physical constraint measured in megawatts or even gigawatts.

At a Fortune 100 bank, I watched a coding agent open a routine session on a payments service. Before the developer typed a word, the agent had read the repository, including the .env file. Production database credentials had entered the agent’s working context, potentially exposing them to a model provider the bank had never assessed. Whether the credentials left the environment depended on controls nobody had verified. Nothing malicious happened. The agent did what it was built to do. That is the problem.

My argument is simple. AI coding-agent vendors and their downstream dependencies form a supplier ecosystem, not just another developer tool. They need the same four control disciplines applied to other privileged suppliers. Govern vendor terms and downstream dependencies. Limit the secrets they hold. Approve the servers they connect to. item.title: 🟠 How to deliver real data sovereignty
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

Changing where your data is stored isn’t enough to deliver sovereignty. You also need to implement the technologies that enforce real control. Local providers are keen to promise alternatives but US ones are making the effort to give customers more options without losing access to the depth of services they offer. Actually turning the promise of sovereign cloud regions into reality means dealing with encryption keys, access workflows and confidential computing, which also means more costs, dependencies, and operational responsibilities.

The obvious concern with using US cloud services is the CLOUD Act, which allows the US government to request access to customer data from a US-owned service, even if it’s held in the EU. Those requests are supposed to go through the criminal court system. “When it lands in Europe it headbutts with GPDR and you’re involved in legal wrangling as to whether or not that data can be released or not,” IDC research director Rahiel Nasir says.

item.title: 🔴 The code and the court: Why your email security thinks like Napoleon
item.description:

In 1804, Napoleon gave France a code that much of the world still runs on. The Code civil replaced a tangle of local customs with a single written statute: orderly and knowable. In that tradition, the judge’s job, in Montesquieu’s phrase, is to be the mouth of the law, nothing more. Certainty was the point.

Certainty has a cost. A codified system is only as current as its code. When the world produces something the code did not anticipate — a new technology, a new fraud — there is no statute to apply, and everyone waits for someone to write one.

Your email security works exactly this way. That is the problem.

Security by statute

A signature is a statute. Someone observes an attack, writes a rule that describes it, and from that moment you are protected against that attack and its close relatives. It is fast, certain, and blind to anything the code has not been written to see.

item.description:

The UK’s digital watchdogs have warned enterprises that they can’t evade their legal responsibilities by blaming errors on AI agents that they have deployed.

“By taking action on behalf of users, such as making purchases and communicating with businesses, these agents could transform how people use digital services, engage with markets and unlock wider innovation,” said the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF), a body comprising the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), and communications regulator Ofcom, in a joint statement.

While the DRCF welcomed such uses it advised, “firms developing or deploying personal agents should think carefully about how consumers can understand when and how an agent acts on their behalf, how authority to act is given and how their personal data is used.”

item.title: 🟠 The CIO’s trust paradox: Your team may be more honest with AI than with you
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

As a leader, you’ve probably spent years nudging your managers to create psychological safety. After all, organizations benefit greatly when it feels safe to challenge the boss, surface bad news early, and say the uncomfortable thing before it becomes the expensive thing.

The Space Shuttle Challenger disaster of 1986 has become the canonical warning. Engineers raised concerns about the O-rings used in the solid rocket booster before launch. Their warnings were overruled by managers under schedule pressure. Seventy-three seconds after liftoff, seven astronauts were dead. The lesson still holds: When people are afraid to speak or are pressured to comply, organizations miss what they already know.

AI, however, is introducing a complication most leaders haven’t accounted for. Your employees now have another place to speak, and emerging research suggests they may be more willing to challenge a machine than a human leader, while another body of research challenges our assumptions about psychological safety itself.

A chain of avoidable technical and human security failures enabled the largest crypto heist on record, the theft of approximately $6.34 billion from Binance. The attackers were then able to pivot through an internal AI tool to additional developer systems, obtain an access token, and deploy a container on Binance’s infrastructure before executing the rogue withdrawals.

item.description:

item.title: 🔵 How to balance governance and innovation in the agentic AI era
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

The conversation about agentic AI is shifting: Rather than focusing solely on what the technology can produce, IT leaders are now considering what they are prepared to let it do. 

Unlike traditional AI assistants that primarily respond to user prompts, agentic AI systems can make decisions and execute actions autonomously across business processes. This creates opportunities to accelerate workflows and improve productivity but also introduces new challenges involving risk and organizational readiness.

The shift is already well under way. In a recent HCLTech survey, 87% of the participating enterprises reported using generative or agentic AI in IT operations, underscoring the growing importance of effective governance. These challenges were central to a recent HCLTech and Google Cloud roundtable on the business impact of agentic AI in which the participants explored what it takes to move from experimentation toward enterprise-wide adoption.

item.description:

Linux administrators’ trust in package managers is being tested by a newly disclosed vulnerability in APT, the package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and their derivatives, that could allow attackers to install unverified software with root privileges.

Tracked as CVE-2026-109518, the vulnerability could let an attacker positioned to manipulate HTTP traffic between an APT client and an archive server install an attacker-controlled package without verification.

Debian disclosed the flaw on November 4, crediting security researcher Max Justicz. Ubuntu subsequently rated it High, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.7.

item.description:

Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network information and hashed root credentials. The attack began around August 17, according to cybersecurity firm GreyNoise, but researchers initially blamed a different vulnerability that Zyxel had already addressed.

The newly identified flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-107441, is a CVSS 8.8 out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the switches’ web management interface. It allows unauthenticated attackers with network access to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 models, including GS1900-8, GS1900-24, and GS1900-48. Zyxel listed firmware versions ending in .2C0 and earlier as vulnerable, with model-specific fixes in versions ending in .3C0.

item.description:

Most SOCs begin their response by calling or messaging the user via Teams to ask whether the 2:00 am sign-in from an unfamiliar country was indeed them. Their subsequent actions depend upon what the user responds with.

Try that with a service account, and you’ll be waiting a long time. item.description:

AI agents help Joe Sandbox uncover malicious behavior concealed by evasion techniques and unmet execution conditions.

Joe Security‘s Adaptive Detonation brings active intervention to malware analysis, helping security teams investigate threats that may conceal their behavior during an initial sandbox run.

Adaptive Detonation uses AI agents to examine execution results, identify obstacles preventing a sample from revealing relevant behavior, and select targeted interventions. These can include patching a blocking check, creating required files or settings, adjusting the execution environment, or supplying missing command-line arguments.

Joe Sandbox then analyzes the sample again under the modified conditions to verify whether the intervention reveals additional activity.

The kinks in the software supply chain are once again being exposed, with attackers now targeting OpsShield’s update process.

This week, threat actors used compromised credentials to push malicious updates out to cPGuard customers. They then accessed data stored on the vendor’s servers and in its billing portal accounts, and made copies of at least three of OpsShield’s cloud servers.

The company said in an advisory that it has “shut the attacker out of every system we know they reached, and … are rebuilding the ones we cannot fully trust.” It has also released updates and urges customers to update to the latest version of cPGuard, change passwords, and generate new SSH keys.

item.title: 🟠 CrowdStrike’s AI SOC vision evolves as agentic uncertainty adds new twist
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

“The software we use has become an actor,” declared CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas in his address on the dangers and opportunity of agentic AI at the company’s Fal.Con conference in September. It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given.

For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this. Agents still work on behalf of humans, but they don’t always reason or act like them. They are entities with capabilities and an unpredictability unlike any threat businesses have ever faced.

item.title: 🟠 Barracuda’s security appliances have a security problem of their own
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself.

The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices.

They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities.

Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately.
